reasoning.Student A:
My true preference is x > w > y > z. I want to maximize my chances of getting into the best school possible according to my preferences. I need to consider the priorities at each school and the preferences of other applicants.

School x: I have priority 2. Many applicants favor y > x > w > z. If I propose to x, I might be rejected if someone with higher priority also proposes to x.
School y: I have priority 1. If I propose to y, I will be tentatively accepted.
School z: I have priority 2.

Scenario 1: I rank according to my true preferences: x > w > y > z
- Round 1: propose to x. I may be rejected. If rejected, propose to w.
- Round 2: propose to w. I will be accepted.
This guarantees me w.

Scenario 2: I rank w first: w > x > y > z
- Round 1: propose to w. I will be accepted.
This guarantees me w.

Scenario 3: I rank y first: y > x > w > z
- Round 1: propose to y. I will be accepted.
This guarantees me y.

Scenario 4: I rank x first, then y: x > y > w > z
- Round 1: propose to x. I may be rejected. If rejected, propose to y.
- Round 2: propose to y. I will be accepted.
This guarantees me y, or x if I wasn't rejected.

Since most applicants favor y > x > w > z, it is likely that x will be competitive and I may be rejected in the first round. If I'm rejected from x, I would ideally want to go to w, since w > y. To ensure I get w if I'm rejected from x, I should rank x > w > y > z.

Therefore, I will rank x > w > y > z.
